# Selection and Manipulation
## Overview
Selection and Manipulation enables users to identify specific subsets of volumetric data or graphical primitives for modification, highlighting, or analysis, and to interactively alter their geometric or visual properties [G]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Cropping and Clipping by focusing on semantic or spatial selection of data elements rather than global view frustum or plane-based visibility culling, allowing for targeted editing and complex interaction states [G].
## Shared principles

## Subtopics

### [Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes](10912-brushing-and-linking-with-hilbert-codes.md)
This method connects 1D visualization views with 3D volume rendering by using Hilbert space-filling curve codes to define selection ranges. It differs from standard spatial selection by mapping the selection criterion to a 1D range of Hilbert codes rather than a 3D bounding box, allowing for compact representation of non-contiguous spatial regions. Choose this when working with structured-regular or AMR data where 1D data views are available and efficient transmission of selection ranges is required.

### [3D Widget Interaction Model](11643-3d-widget-interaction-model.md)
The 3D Widget Interaction Model provides a framework for creating interactive, scene-represented objects that users can directly manipulate to control visualization parameters or data processing pipelines [G]. It distinguishes itself from siblings by decoupling interaction handling from camera control and associating a visual representation with the widget, allowing the widget's state to drive downstream data transformations via an event-driven observer pattern [G]. Choose this when a robust, event-driven framework for creating and manipulating 3D graphical handles is needed.

### [Lock Tool](13353-lock-tool.md)
The Lock Tool is an interaction mechanism that specifies data points immune to modification by subsequent brush or dig tools, allowing users to protect specific data subsets during volumetric exploration. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Brushing and Linking with Hilbert Codes by operating on a binary visibility state (locked/unlocked) rather than continuous selection weights, and from the 3D Widget Interaction Model by focusing on data subset protection rather than geometric transformation. Choose this when isolating regions of interest from accidental modification or visual clutter during interactive volume rendering is required.

### Direct Selection and Deletion
**Definition:** An approach where users instantly highlight all splats that intersect with the brush during selection, contrasting with indirect approaches that compute intersections after brushing [S1].
**Steps:** Selection/deletion brushes may be either circular (screen space) or spherical (world space) [S1]. Users may choose selections based on splat centers or their border [S1]. In case of circular brushes and splat-border intersection tests, apply an approximation that checks whether the center of the brush circle is inside an ellipse that is enlarged by the radius of the brush [S1]. Sort all splats by their deletion flag, putting the deleted splats towards the end of the buffer [S1]. Unmap and release physical allocations at the buffer's end in steps of the GPU's granularity [S1].
**Pitfalls:** Using radix sort is not required; developers may implement this functionality with GPU-friendly stream compaction [S1].

### Selection Interaction States
**Definition:** Integrated: Selection acts as fully belonging to the 3D scene. Movement depends on distance to origin; can move out of viewport or be occluded [S2]. Decoupled: Selection fully decoupled from scene. Independently manipulated, not affected by viewing transformation. Useful for fixed orientation [S2]. Pinned: Hybrid mode. Object pinned to current image space position. On-screen location static, but affected by rotations (same relative rotation as viewpoint) [S2].

### Image Plane Selection
**Definition:** A selection technique where 3D objects are projected onto a 2D image plane, and a cursor defines a perpendicular ray to select the first intersected object [S3, unofficial]. A selection technique where users select objects that visually lie behind a hand-attached cursor, defined by the vector joining the user's eye and hand [S3, unofficial].
**Steps:** For stereoscopic displays, define the image plane as the viewpoint from only a single eye to create a one-eyed cursor [S3, unofficial]. Aperture-based variant: Cast cone from eye through finger [S3, unofficial]. Distance between finger and eye controls cone divergence angle [S3, unofficial]. Use device orientation for disambiguation when multiple objects intersect [S3, unofficial]. Head Crusher: Select objects lying between index finger and thumb [S3, unofficial]. Sticky Finger: Select objects occluded by the tip of the index finger [S3, unofficial]. Lifting Palm: Flatten hand and position palm underneath object to select it [S3, unofficial]. Framing Hands: Use both hands to define a bounding box around object using thumbs and index fingers [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The concepts of selection and manipulation in volume rendering and 3D visualization have evolved from simple ray-casting techniques to complex, state-aware interaction models [S3, unofficial]. Early work on image plane selection and ray cursors established the foundation for 3D interaction [S3, unofficial]. Direct selection techniques, particularly for emerging media like Gaussian Splatting, emphasize immediate visual feedback to enhance user experience in interactive editing tasks [S1]. The 3D Widget Interaction Model relies on the VTK command/observer pattern to bridge user input gestures with specific application logic [G].
